assertion: Apple — Apples are the fruits of cultivated trees in the genus Malus.
Banana — Bananas grow in hanging clusters and many dessert varieties develop a yellow peel as they ripen.
Orange — The sweet orange is a segmented citrus fruit with an aromatic peel.
Pineapple — A pineapple develops from many flowers into one compound fruit topped by leaves.
Pomegranate — A pomegranate encloses numerous juicy arils around its seeds.
Carrot — The cultivated carrot is grown mainly for its enlarged edible taproot.
Onion — The common onion stores nutrients in fleshy leaf bases that form its layered bulb.
Radish — Radishes are edible roots whose familiar red varieties have crisp white flesh and a peppery flavour.
Broccoli — A broccoli head consists mainly of immature flower clusters on thick stalks.
Asparagus — Edible asparagus spears are young shoots cut before their branches unfold.
Thyme — The traditional song lists parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme, all familiar culinary herbs.
Dill — Dill's leaves and seeds are aromatic and widely used in pickling and fish cookery.
Mint — Menthol activates cold-sensitive receptors, giving mint its cooling sensation.
Coriander — Cilantro and coriander leaves are names for the fresh foliage of Coriandrum sativum.
Rosemary — Rosemary is an evergreen aromatic shrub with narrow leaves used in cooking.
Cinnamon — Cinnamon comes from dried inner bark of trees in the genus Cinnamomum.
Black pepper — Black pepper is made from dried fruits of the pepper vine.
Saffron — Saffron threads are the hand-collected stigmas of the saffron crocus.
Clove — Culinary cloves are dried flower buds of the clove tree.
Turmeric — Turmeric powder is made from the dried rhizome of Curcuma longa.
Baguette — A baguette is a characteristically long French bread with a lean dough and crisp crust.
Pita — Steam can separate the layers of pita during baking and create a hollow pocket.
Naan — Naan dough is stretched and slapped onto the hot inner wall of a tandoor oven.
Corn tortilla — A corn tortilla is a flatbread made from treated maize dough called masa.
Injera — Injera is a fermented, pancake-like flatbread served beneath and alongside stews.
Mozzarella — Mozzarella melts smoothly and is central to many Italian pizzas.
Cheddar — Cheddar takes its name from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England.
Feta — EU-protected feta is a Greek brined cheese made from sheep's milk or a sheep-and-goat blend.
Brie — Brie is a soft cow's-milk cheese ripened under a white mould rind.
Gouda — Gouda cheese is named for the Dutch city where it was historically traded.
Spaghetti — Spaghetti is a long, solid, cylindrical form of pasta.
Penne — Penne is cut on the diagonal, and its name refers to pen nibs or quills.
Farfalle — Farfalle means butterflies in Italian and describes the pasta's winged shape.
Lasagne — Lasagne are wide pasta sheets used in the layered baked dish of the same name.
Ravioli — Ravioli seal fillings such as cheese, meat, or vegetables between thin pasta layers.
Fried rice — Fried rice is made by stir-frying cooked rice with seasonings and varied additions.
Rice pudding — Rice pudding combines cooked rice with milk or cream and a sweetener.
Risotto — Risotto develops a creamy texture as short-grain rice releases starch into added broth.
Paella — Paella is a Valencian rice dish named after the broad pan used to cook it.
Biryani — Biryani combines seasoned rice with a separately prepared meat or vegetable component.
Tomato soup — Tomato soup uses tomatoes as its primary ingredient and may be smooth or chunky.
French onion soup — French onion soup combines deeply browned onions with stock and a gratinéed bread topping.
Miso soup — Miso soup is prepared by mixing miso paste into a dashi-based broth.
Borscht — Many familiar forms of borscht use beetroot as the ingredient that gives the soup its red colour.
Gazpacho — Gazpacho is served cold and is built from blended raw vegetables and olive oil.
Caesar salad — A classic Caesar salad is based on dressed romaine leaves, croutons, and Parmesan.
Greek salad — Greek salad, or horiatiki, combines fresh vegetables with olives and feta.
Coleslaw — Coleslaw dresses shredded cabbage, often together with carrot.
Caprese salad — Caprese salad pairs tomatoes and mozzarella with fresh basil and olive oil.
Waldorf salad — The familiar Waldorf combination includes apple, celery, walnuts, and mayonnaise.
Porridge — Porridge is a soft cereal dish produced by boiling grain in liquid.
Waffle — A waffle iron presses batter into a crisp cake with a distinctive grid pattern.
Croissant — Croissant dough is laminated with butter, creating airy layers during baking.
Muesli — Muesli is a loose mixture of grains and additions served with milk, yoghurt, or fruit.
Eggs Benedict — Eggs Benedict combines toasted muffin halves, a savoury layer, poached eggs, and hollandaise.
Tiramisu — Tiramisu layers coffee-dipped ladyfingers with a mascarpone-based mixture.
Crème brûlée — Crème brûlée contrasts a chilled custard base with a hard caramel top.
Apple pie — Apple pie surrounds seasoned apple pieces with pastry, often above and below.
Cheesecake — Cheesecake uses a sweetened soft-cheese filling set over a pastry or crumb base.
Baklava — Baklava is assembled from many filo layers, a nut filling, and syrup or honey.
Ganache — Ganache forms when chopped chocolate melts into warm cream and the mixture becomes a smooth emulsion.
Cocoa butter — Cocoa butter is the natural fat separated from cacao beans.
Dark chocolate — Dark chocolate is based on cocoa solids and cocoa butter with sugar, without the milk component of milk chocolate.
White chocolate — White chocolate contains cocoa butter but not the dark cocoa particles found in other varieties.
Tempering — Tempering encourages stable cocoa-butter crystals that create shine and a firm texture.
Gelato — Gelato is the Italian style of churned frozen dairy dessert.
Sorbet — Sorbet freezes fruit purée or juice with sugar and water rather than milk or cream.
Sundae — A sundae is a dish of frozen scoops dressed with sweet toppings.
Vanilla — Vanilla flavour comes from cured seed pods of orchids in the genus Vanilla.
Churning — Churning keeps the mixture moving, breaks up ice crystals, and incorporates air.
French press — A French press steeps coarse grounds in hot water and then separates them with a plunger-mounted filter.
Cappuccino — A cappuccino is built from espresso and textured milk with a distinct foamed top.
Caffè latte — Caffè latte means coffee with milk and combines espresso with a larger milk component.
Caffè Americano — Adding hot water to espresso produces the longer drink known as an Americano.
Coffee cherry — Coffee beans are seeds found inside the fruit commonly called a coffee cherry.
Black tea — Black-tea processing allows substantial leaf oxidation, creating its darker colour and flavour.
Green tea — Early heating stops most oxidation in green-tea leaves.
Herbal tea — Herbal teas are infusions of plants other than the tea plant.
Oolong — Oolong processing uses controlled partial oxidation to create a wide range of aromas.
Matcha — With matcha, shade-grown leaves are ground and consumed as part of the drink.
Pineapple juice — Pineapple juice is pressed from the sweet flesh of the tropical pineapple fruit.
Apple juice — Apple juice is extracted by crushing and pressing apples, then often filtering or pasteurising it.
Tomato juice — Tomato juice preserves the fruit's pulp and savoury flavour in drinkable form.
Cranberry juice — Cranberries are tart wetland berries whose juice is commonly blended or sweetened.
Grapefruit juice — Grapefruits grow in clusters and produce a juice with both sharp acidity and bitter compounds.
Whisk — A whisk's loops move rapidly through liquid to blend it and trap air bubbles.
Grater — Food rubbed across a grater's cutting holes is reduced to small shreds.
Peeler — A peeler cuts away a thin surface layer while following the shape of produce.
Colander — A colander retains solid food while liquid escapes through its holes.
Mortar and pestle — The pestle presses and grinds ingredients against the hard interior of the mortar.
Boiling — Boiling transfers heat from vigorously moving hot liquid into the food.
Steaming — Steam condenses on the food and transfers heat without the food sitting in water.
Sautéing — Sautéing uses high direct heat, a shallow pan, and a small amount of fat.
Roasting — Roasting surrounds food with dry heat that promotes browning at the surface.
Poaching — Poaching uses relatively calm hot liquid to cook delicate food without vigorous bubbling.
Baker's yeast — Baker's yeast ferments sugars in dough and fills it with carbon-dioxide bubbles.
Baking powder — Moisture activates baking powder's acid-base reaction and releases carbon dioxide.
Kneading — Kneading aligns and strengthens gluten proteins so dough can trap gas.
Proofing — During proofing, fermentation continues and gas expands the dough's structure.
Blind baking — Blind baking sets and browns pastry before a wet or unbaked filling is added.
Pizza Margherita — Pizza Margherita uses tomato, mozzarella, and fresh basil as its signature toppings.
Pesto — Pesto alla genovese is pounded or blended from fresh basil and its traditional partners.
Gnocchi — Potato gnocchi combine cooked potato with enough flour to form tender dumplings.
Polenta — Polenta is cooked maize meal that can be served soft or cooled until firm.
Affogato — Affogato al caffè pairs cold gelato with freshly poured espresso.
Taco — A taco uses a small tortilla to hold meat, vegetables, salsa, or other fillings.
Guacamole — Guacamole combines mashed avocado with seasonings such as lime, chilli, onion, or coriander.
Salsa — Salsa simply means sauce in Spanish and includes many fresh and cooked Mexican varieties.
Tamale — A tamal is a parcel of maize dough steamed in a leaf wrapper.
Mole — Mole is a family of richly seasoned sauces rather than one fixed recipe.
Sushi — The defining element of sushi is vinegared rice combined with toppings, fillings, or seaweed.
Sashimi — Sashimi consists of sliced raw fish or other seafood served on its own with garnishes.
Tempura — Tempura uses a thin batter and hot oil to create a light, crisp coating.
Miso — Miso fermentation combines soybeans, salt, and kōji culture into an umami-rich paste.
Ramen — Ramen combines Chinese-style wheat noodles with seasoned broth and toppings.
Cinnamon bun — Cinnamon buns are rolled around a cinnamon filling and are a familiar Nordic bakery treat.
Swedish meatballs — Swedish meatballs are commonly served with cream gravy, potatoes, and lingonberry jam.
Skyr — Skyr is cultured from milk and strained into a thick fresh dairy product.
Gravlax — Gravlax is salmon cured without smoking in a mixture typically flavoured with dill.
Salmon soup — Finnish salmon soup, or lohikeitto, cooks salmon and potatoes in a creamy broth flavoured with dill.
Kama — Kama is a ready-to-eat blend of roasted grain and pea flours used in quick dairy desserts.
Rye bread — Dense sourdough rye breads are central to the food traditions of all three Baltic countries.
Curd snack — The Baltic curd snack combines a sweet pressed-curd centre with a thin confectionery coating.
Šaltibarščiai — Šaltibarščiai is served cold and gets its pink colour when beetroot is mixed with cultured dairy.
Grey peas and bacon — Grey peas with bacon and onion are a traditional Latvian hot dish.
Toaster — A toaster exposes bread slices to radiant heat until their surfaces brown.
Scrambled eggs — Scrambled eggs form soft curds when beaten eggs are stirred during cooking.
Granola — Granola is baked until its grains, nuts, and sweetener form crisp clusters.
Shakshuka — Shakshuka poaches eggs in a sauce of tomatoes, peppers, onions, and spices.
Congee — Congee is made by cooking rice in abundant water until the grains soften into porridge.
Popcorn — Steam pressure bursts a popcorn kernel and rapidly expands its cooked starch.
Lemon juice — Lemon juice is acidic and contains antioxidants that slow enzymatic browning.
Mayonnaise — Egg-yolk emulsifiers help mayonnaise hold oil and water together.
Pressure cooker — A pressure cooker traps steam, allowing water and food to reach a higher temperature.
Aquafaba — Aquafaba contains dissolved starches and proteins that let it trap air as a foam.
Oven — An oven surrounds food with controlled heat for baking and roasting.
Rolling pin — A rolling pin spreads dough into a thinner, even sheet.
Baking paper — Baking parchment provides a heat-resistant, non-stick surface on a tray.
Piping bag — A piping bag pushes soft icing or dough through a shaped nozzle.
Bain-marie — A bain-marie surrounds a container with hot water to moderate the heat.
Watermelon — A watermelon is a large melon with a hard rind and water-rich flesh.
Kiwifruit — Kiwifruit was given its commercial name after New Zealand’s kiwi bird.
Strawberry — The visible specks on a strawberry are small fruits called achenes.
Avocado — Avocado flesh surrounds one large seed and is mashed for guacamole.
Fig — A fig’s enclosed flower structure develops into the fleshy multiple fruit we eat.
Rice — Rice is a cereal grain cooked as a staple food across much of the world.
Pasta — Many dried pasta shapes are made from durum-wheat semolina and water.
Lentils — Lentils are edible pulse seeds that come in several colours and cook without soaking.
Couscous — Couscous is made by rolling moistened semolina into small granules and steaming them.
Bulgur — Bulgur is made from wheat groats that are parboiled, dried, and cracked.
Lemon zest — Lemon zest is the aromatic outer layer of the peel.
Soy sauce — Soy sauce is a fermented liquid seasoning made chiefly from soybeans and wheat.
Sesame oil — Toasted sesame oil has a strong nutty aroma and is commonly used as a finishing flavour.
Capers — Capers are unopened flower buds preserved in salt or brine.
Harissa — Harissa is a North African chilli paste seasoned with garlic and spices.
Lid — A fitted lid can exclude oxygen from a small contained cooking fire.
Kitchen timer — A kitchen timer sounds after a chosen interval so a cook need not watch the clock.
Ice bath — An ice bath cools blanched food rapidly and limits further cooking.
Slurry — Starch dispersed in cold liquid can thicken a hot sauce without forming dry lumps.
Deglazing — Deglazing dissolves browned pan residue so it can flavour a sauce.
Brownie — A brownie is a dense chocolate bake usually served as a square or bar.
Meringue — Meringue is a sweet foam made by whipping egg whites and sugar.
Churros — Churros are piped lengths of dough fried until crisp and commonly dusted with sugar.
Panna cotta — Panna cotta is sweetened cream set with gelatine in a mould or serving glass.
Profiterole — A profiterole is a filled choux-pastry ball, commonly served with chocolate sauce.
table reservation — A table reservation is a booking made before arrival so a restaurant keeps a table available for the diners.
drive-through — A drive-through serves customers while they remain in their vehicle for ordering and collection.
buffet — A buffet offers several shared dishes from which diners serve themselves.
canteen — A canteen is a simple place at a school or workplace where people usually select and collect their own food.
service charge — A service charge is a fee added to a restaurant bill for providing service.
KFC — KFC is a fast-food chain known for bucket meals and a recipe described as a blend of eleven herbs and spices.
Oreo — An Oreo has two dark biscuit pieces around a pale sweet filling and is often eaten by twisting the halves apart.
Heinz — Heinz is a food brand whose ketchup has long been associated with the “57 varieties” slogan.
Nescafé — Nescafé is Nestlé's instant-coffee brand, and its name combines Nestlé with the French word café.
Kellogg's — Kellogg's is the breakfast-cereal company behind brands including Frosties and Coco Pops.
fish and chips — Fish and chips pairs battered fried fish with thick-cut fried potatoes and is a well-known British takeaway meal.
chicken nuggets — Chicken nuggets are small pieces of poultry meat that are breaded and cooked as bite-size fast food.
fried chicken — Fried chicken consists of poultry pieces such as wings or drumsticks coated and cooked in hot oil until crisp.
onion rings — Onion rings are round slices of onion coated in batter or crumbs and fried.
doner kebab — Doner kebab is a Turkish dish of seasoned meat cooked on a vertical rotisserie, sliced off and commonly served in flatbread.
wasabi — Wasabi is a pungent green Japanese paste with a flavour often compared with hot mustard or horseradish.
dim sum — Dim sum is a Cantonese meal of small dishes traditionally shared at the table with tea.
teriyaki — Teriyaki is a Japanese cooking style in which food is given a glossy glaze based on soy sauce and sugar.
udon — Udon is a thick Japanese noodle made from wheat flour and commonly served in broth.
wonton soup — Wonton soup is a Chinese broth containing small dough parcels wrapped around a filling.
instant noodles — Instant noodles are dried noodles sold with seasoning in a packet or cup and prepared in minutes with hot water.
frozen pizza — This prepared topped round is stored below zero and baked before eating.
ready meal — A ready meal is a fresh or frozen prepackaged dish that only needs heating, sometimes in its own packaging.
energy bar — An energy bar is a compact packaged snack designed to provide food energy conveniently.
microwave popcorn — Microwave popcorn comes as kernels in a folded paper bag that expands while the kernels pop during heating.
cabbage rolls — Cabbage rolls are cooked cabbage leaves wrapped around a savoury filling that often combines meat and grain.
mac and cheese — Mac and cheese combines cooked macaroni with a creamy cheese sauce.
chicken soup — Chicken soup is a warm broth made with poultry and is commonly eaten as comfort food during a cold.
meatloaf — Meatloaf is made by shaping seasoned minced meat into a loaf and baking it.
grilled cheese sandwich — A grilled cheese sandwich is made by browning bread around a filling dominated by melted cheese.
potato chips — Potato chips are thin slices of potato cooked until crisp and commonly sold salted in bags.
potato wedges — Potato wedges are thick lengthwise pieces of potato, often left with the skin on, then baked or fried.
gummy bears — Gummy bears are small, chewy, colourful sweets moulded into the shape of bears.
mozzarella sticks — Mozzarella sticks are elongated pieces of mozzarella coated in batter or breadcrumbs and usually served as an appetiser.
cheese puffs — Cheese puffs are airy puffed-corn snacks covered with cheese-flavoured powder.
Popeye — Popeye is a cartoon sailor whose strength increases after he eats canned leafy greens.
Ronald McDonald — Ronald McDonald is the clown character used as the primary mascot of a global fast-food chain.
Cookie Monster — Cookie Monster is the furry blue Sesame Street puppet known for his enthusiastic appetite for baked treats.
Joey Tribbiani — Joey Tribbiani is Matt LeBlanc's food-loving sitcom character, remembered for insisting that he does not share food.
Mr. Krabs — Mr. Krabs is a money-loving red crab who owns an underwater fast-food restaurant.
cake mix — A cake mix is a powdered blend of dry ingredients prepared for making a cake.
chocolate chips — Chocolate chips are small shaped pieces of chocolate made to be mixed into dough or batter for baking.
cocoa powder — Cocoa powder is an unsweetened brown product of cacao beans used to give baked goods a chocolate flavour.
cornstarch — Cornstarch is a fine white starch made from maize and commonly used to thicken sauces.
vanilla extract — Vanilla extract is a flavouring liquid made by soaking or macerating vanilla pods in alcohol and water.
lactose-free milk — Lactose-free milk is treated by removing its lactose or breaking that sugar down with an enzyme.
cottage cheese — Cottage cheese is a mild fresh cheese made of small, visible curds and often packaged in a tub.
whole milk — Whole milk retains its normal milk-fat level rather than having fat reduced through the removal of cream.
smoked cheese — Smoked cheese is exposed to smoke, which gives it a characteristic flavour and often a brownish outer colour.
quark — Quark is a soft white unaged dairy product made by souring milk and straining the resulting curds.
tap water — Tap water is drinking water supplied through indoor plumbing to a faucet.
flavoured water — Flavoured water is non-carbonated water with added flavouring and may also include sweeteners or vitamins.
energy drink — Energy drinks are marketed to increase alertness and commonly contain caffeine.
vegetable juice — Vegetable juice is made by blending vegetables or extracting their liquid; carrots and tomatoes are common ingredients.
coconut water — Coconut water is the clear liquid naturally found inside young green coconuts.
peeling — Peeling is the action of removing an outer skin or layer from food.
grating — Grating reduces food to small shreds by rubbing it against a surface with sharp projections or holes.
sieving — Sieving passes an ingredient through a mesh so that lumps or larger particles are left behind.
meat tenderising — Meat tenderising can be done mechanically by pounding a piece so it becomes less tough.
garnishing — Garnishing means adding a decorative edible element to food before it is served.
freezer — A freezer is an appliance or compartment that keeps food frozen at very low temperatures.
cling film — Cling film is a thin transparent plastic sheet used to cover food and seal containers.
zipper storage bag — A zipper storage bag is a flexible plastic pouch closed by pressing together two interlocking tracks.
glass jar — A glass jar is a rigid wide-mouthed container with a lid, commonly used for preserves.
pantry — A pantry is a small room or cupboard used to store food, groceries and kitchen supplies.
ingredients list — An ingredients list tells consumers which substances were used to make a packaged food.
nutrition label — A nutrition label reports a food's energy value and amounts of nutrients such as fat, carbohydrate and protein.
allergen warning — An allergen warning highlights substances in a food that may cause allergic reactions.
serving size — EU rules allow nutrition values per serving or consumption unit in addition to the standard values per 100 grams or millilitres.
best-before date — A best-before date concerns food quality, while a use-by date concerns safety for highly perishable food.

assertion: Swiss roll — A Swiss roll is a thin filled sponge cake rolled into a cylinder and sliced to show a spiral.
cupcake — A cupcake is a small cake designed for one person and is often topped with icing or decorations.
doughnut — A doughnut is a sweet fried pastry that is often shaped like a ring with a central hole.
marble cake — Marble cake gets its streaked appearance by lightly mixing pale and chocolate batters.
banana bread — Banana bread is a moist loaf-shaped bake made with mashed ripe bananas.
birthday candles — Birthday candles are placed on a cake and traditionally blown out after the celebrant makes a wish.
cocktail cherry — A cocktail cherry, also called a maraschino cherry, is a preserved sweet cherry placed as decoration on cakes, ice cream and drinks.
edible flowers — Edible flowers are blossoms that can safely be eaten and used to add colour and decoration to food.
fondant — Fondant is a smooth sweet paste that can be rolled flat and used to cover or decorate cakes.
royal icing — Royal icing is a hard white icing made from softly beaten egg whites and powdered sugar.
kitchen apron — A kitchen apron is tied over clothing to protect it from splashes, spills and other messes.
oven mitt — An oven mitt is an insulated hand covering used to handle hot cookware safely.
muffin tin — A muffin tin is a metal baking pan with several round cups for baking individual small cakes.
kitchen scales — Kitchen scales are used to weigh recipe ingredients, commonly in grams.
pastry brush — A pastry brush is a small kitchen brush used to spread egg wash, butter or glaze over food.
Pepsi — Pepsi uses a red, white and blue circular logo known as the Pepsi Globe.
Fanta — Fanta is a five-letter fruit-flavoured fizzy-drink brand that includes an orange product.
Sprite — Sprite is a clear lemon-lime soft drink with a six-letter brand name beginning with S and ending in “ite”.
Schweppes — Schweppes is a long-running carbonated-drink brand founded by Jacob Schweppe.
7 Up — 7 Up is a lemon-lime soft-drink brand that was advertised using the character Fido Dido.
maple syrup — Maple syrup is made by concentrating sap collected from maple trees.
stevia — Stevia plants provide leaf extracts that are used as high-intensity sweeteners.
sugar cube — A sugar cube is made by pressing white sugar granules into a small cube, commonly used to sweeten tea or coffee.
vanilla sugar — Vanilla sugar is made by infusing sugar with vanilla beans or by mixing the grains with liquid flavouring from the same plant, and it is common in European desserts.
jam sugar — Jam sugar combines sugar with a gelling agent for making preserves, helping cooked fruit mixtures reach the desired consistency.
lemonade — Lemonade is commonly made by mixing lemon juice with water and a sweetener.
smoothie — A smoothie is a thick cold drink made by blending puréed fruit with a liquid.
iced coffee — Iced coffee is brewed coffee served cold and commonly poured over ice.
hot chocolate — Hot chocolate is a heated drink made with cocoa or melted chocolate.
fruit punch — Fruit punch is a usually non-alcoholic mixture of fruit juices served as punch, often from a communal bowl.
frittata — A frittata cooks its eggs and fillings together as a thick, open-faced dish, often with the top set under direct heat.
quiche — Quiche is an open pastry case with a savoury egg-and-dairy filling; quiche Lorraine traditionally adds lardons or bacon.
tortilla española — Tortilla española slowly sets eggs around fried potatoes and often onion, producing a thick cake cut into wedges.
chawanmushi — Chawanmushi means 'steamed in a tea bowl' and differs from sweet custards through its dashi-based savoury filling.
menemen — Menemen cooks eggs with tomatoes, peppers, and seasonings into a soft mixture intended for sharing with bread.
pelmeni — Pelmeni are boiled from fresh or frozen and traditionally use a compact meat filling inside unleavened dough.
pierogi — Pierogi are filled Polish dumplings whose many savoury and sweet versions are boiled before optional pan-frying.
gyōza — The popular yaki-gyōza method gives the base a crisp crust while steam cooks the wrapper and filling.
xiaolongbao — Xiaolongbao enclose meat and chilled gelled stock; the stock melts into soup during steaming.
manti — Manti belong to a broad family of Turkic and Central Asian filled dumplings with regional shapes and sauces.
pretzel — The alkaline treatment gives a pretzel its dark glossy crust and distinctive flavour while its knotted shape remains recognizable.
goulash — Gulyás began as a herders' dish; paprika became a defining flavour after the spice spread through Hungarian cooking.
Wiener schnitzel — A true Wiener schnitzel uses veal; similar breaded cutlets made from pork are normally labelled by the meat used.
apple strudel — Apple strudel rolls sliced apples and spices inside an exceptionally thin sheet of stretched dough.
raclette — Raclette names both the meltable cheese and the communal dish made by scraping its heated surface onto accompaniments.
satay — Satay developed in Java and spread across Southeast Asia, where meats, marinades, and accompanying sauces vary.
laksa — Laksa is a family of noodle soups whose major styles include creamy curry laksa and tart fish-based asam laksa.
rendang — Rendang's long reduction fries the meat in the coconut's released oil, helping the spice coating cling and concentrate.
som tam — Som tam balances sour, hot, sweet, and salty tastes while the firm unripe fruit keeps its crunch.
tom kha gai — The name identifies boiled galangal with chicken, while coconut milk carries the soup's aromatic herbs and sour heat.
dosa — Fermentation gives dosa batter flavour and lift; the batter can be cooked plain or wrapped around a potato filling.
butter chicken — Butter chicken, or murgh makhani, was devised as a way to keep leftover tandoori chicken tender in a rich sauce.
korma — Korma describes a family of mild, aromatic braises whose sauce can be thickened with dairy, nuts, or seeds.
vindaloo — Vindaloo developed from carne de vinha d'alhos; its Goan form uses vinegar, garlic, and a distinctive spice mixture.
gulab jamun — Gulab jamun uses khoya or milk powder for its soft fried dumplings, which absorb warm aromatic syrup.
tagine — A tagine's tall lid returns condensed steam to the stew, allowing slow cooking with relatively little added water.
tabbouleh — Traditional tabbouleh is herb-forward rather than grain-heavy, with parsley providing most of its volume and colour.
baba ghanoush — Charring the aubergine before mixing its flesh with sesame paste gives baba ghanoush its characteristic smokiness.
muhammara — Muhammara is an Aleppo-born dip whose sweet-tart pomegranate molasses balances red pepper and walnuts.
fattoush — Fattoush belongs to the fattat family of dishes that make practical use of pieces of stale or toasted bread.
Black Forest gâteau — Its German name is Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, literally Black Forest cherry cake, reflecting its chocolate, cream, and cherry layers.
Sachertorte — Franz Sacher created the cake in Vienna; its contrast of chocolate and apricot became the signature of the later hotel.
pastel de nata — Pastéis de nata descend from pastéis de Belém, created by Catholic monks at Lisbon's Jerónimos Monastery before the 18th century.
tres leches cake — The airy sponge of tres leches cake absorbs its rich milk mixture without completely falling apart.
lamington — Lamington's thin chocolate coating soaks slightly into the sponge before the coconut forms its dry outer layer.
rhubarb — Rhubarb's fleshy leaf stalk is edible after cooking, whereas the leaf blade contains compounds unsafe to eat.
kohlrabi — Kohlrabi belongs to the cabbage family, but its turnip-like edible part is an enlarged stem.
cashew — The cashew apple is a fleshy false fruit, while the kidney-shaped structure hanging below it contains the commercial seed.
artichoke — The globe artichoke is a cultivated thistle whose immature flower head is eaten before the florets open.
mace — One nutmeg fruit yields two spices: nutmeg from the seed and mace from the dried aril around it.
focaccia — Focaccia genovese is brushed with olive oil and marked with finger-sized dimples before baking.
cacio e pepe — Starchy pasta water helps grated pecorino and pepper form the creamy coating in cacio e pepe without added cream.
arancini — Arancini means little oranges, a reference to the fried rice balls' golden colour and rounded shape.
osso buco — Osso buco means bone with a hole, describing the marrow bone at the centre of the braised veal shank.
ribollita — Ribollita grew from peasant cookery in which leftover vegetable-and-bread soup became richer when cooked again.
tzatziki — Tzatziki is thickened by strained yoghurt and cucumber, while garlic and herbs provide its savoury freshness.
chimichurri — Chimichurri's acidity and fresh herbs cut through the richness of food cooked over an asado fire.
sriracha — Thai sriracha began as a pourable chilli sauce; later international versions can be thicker and sweeter.
romesco — Romesco is pounded or blended into a thick rust-coloured sauce traditionally suited to fish and grilled vegetables.
hoisin sauce — Hoisin is usually based on fermented soybean paste, sweeteners, and spices despite the seafood meaning of its name.
club sandwich — The club sandwich is distinguished by layered toast and a tall filling, making quartering and securing it practical.
Reuben sandwich — The Reuben balances fatty beef and melted cheese with acidic cabbage and dressing on sturdy rye bread.
croque monsieur — A croque monsieur is a hot ham-and-cheese sandwich; adding a fried or poached egg turns it into a croque madame.
smørrebrød — Smørrebrød literally means butter and bread, but its arranged toppings turned it into a distinctive Danish lunch tradition.
muffuletta — The muffuletta takes its name from the Sicilian-style round loaf, while New Orleans' olive salad defines the sandwich filling.
nachos — Nachos began as tortilla chips topped with cheese; restaurateur Ignacio Anaya created the dish in Piedras Negras in 1943.
carpaccio — Giuseppe Cipriani created carpaccio at Harry’s Bar in Venice in 1950 and named it for a Venetian painter.
Peach Melba — Auguste Escoffier invented Peach Melba at London’s Savoy Hotel in honour of singer Nellie Melba.
Salisbury steak — Salisbury steak is an American ground-meat dish commonly served with gravy and named for physician James Salisbury.
Graham cracker — The graham cracker uses graham flour and traces its name to dietary reformer Sylvester Graham.
cheeseburger — A cheeseburger is a hamburger topped with cheese, usually added near the end of cooking so it melts.
hot dog — A hot dog combines a wiener or frankfurter with a slit bun and any of many regional toppings.
Buffalo wings — Buffalo wings are fried without breading, tossed in cayenne hot sauce and butter, and traditionally served with celery and a cooling dip.
corn dog — A corn dog is a sausage on a stick coated in cornmeal batter and deep-fried.
s'more — A s’more is assembled from crisp crackers, toasted marshmallow, and chocolate while the filling is warm.
shepherd's pie — Shepherd’s pie traditionally distinguishes its lamb or mutton filling from the beef filling of cottage pie.
Yorkshire pudding — Yorkshire pudding is a British baked batter dish served in many forms, especially with a Sunday roast.
trifle — Trifle is built in visible layers and allows many variations in its fruit, sponge, custard, and cream.
scone — A scone is a quick bake rather than a yeast bread and is central to the British cream-tea tradition.
Scotch egg — A Scotch egg has three clear layers: boiled egg, sausage meat, and a crisp breadcrumb coating.
moussaka — The modern Greek moussaka is layered, served hot, and commonly finished with a milk-based béchamel layer.
souvlaki — Souvlaki means small pieces of meat grilled on a skewer; in Greece pork is especially common.
dolma — Dolma covers many stuffed vegetables and leaves; leaf-wrapped versions can more precisely be called sarma.
spanakopita — Spanakopita is Greece’s spinach pie, usually pairing the greens with feta or another white cheese.
loukoumades — Loukoumades belong to a wider eastern Mediterranean family of syrup-soaked fried dough known as lokma.
macaron — A Parisian-style macaron uses almond-meringue shells with a ruffled foot and a soft filling.
mille-feuille — Mille-feuille alternates three crisp puff-pastry layers with two layers of pastry cream.
tarte Tatin — Tarte Tatin was named for the Tatin sisters, who served the caramelised upside-down tart at their hotel.
canelé — Canelé is a Bordeaux speciality whose mould creates its recognisable ridged sides and caramelised shell.
Paris–Brest — Paris–Brest combines a wheel-shaped choux ring with nut-flavoured cream and commemorates the Paris–Brest–Paris race.
liquorice — Liquorice flavour is extracted from the root of a legume native to parts of Asia, North Africa, and southern Europe.
fudge — Fudge developed in the 19th-century United States and can be flavoured with chocolate, caramel, fruit, or nuts.
nougat — European white nougat is an egg-white foam sweetened with honey or sugar and set with nuts or candied fruit.
Turkish delight — Turkish delight is a starch-and-sugar gel whose traditional flavours include rosewater, citrus, and mastic.
praline — French praline is firm caramelised sugar with nuts, unlike the softer cream-and-pecan American version.
carrot cake — Carrot cake uses grated carrots in a spiced, oil-based batter that stays moist even when chilled.
red velvet cake — Red velvet cake is a cocoa-and-buttermilk layer cake whose modern colour usually comes from food colouring.
Victoria sponge — Victoria sponge, also called a Victoria sandwich, pairs two sponge layers with jam and often cream, then is finished with a dusting of sugar.
Battenberg cake — Battenberg cake is assembled from coloured sponge sections so its cross-section forms four alternating squares.
angel food cake — Angel food cake gets its lift from egg-white foam and is inverted after baking so its delicate structure does not collapse.
ketchup — Modern ketchup is tomato-based, although earlier recipes used ingredients such as mushrooms, oysters, or walnuts.
barbecue sauce — Barbecue sauce varies by region but commonly starts with vinegar, tomato, or both, plus spices and a sweetener.
tartar sauce — Tartar sauce is especially associated with breaded seafood and gains sharpness from pickles and capers.
Tabasco sauce — Tabasco was created by Edmund McIlhenny in 1868 and is still produced by his company on Avery Island.
aioli — Traditional aioli emulsifies garlic with olive oil; many modern versions also use egg yolk and lemon juice.
peanut butter — Peanut butter is ground from dry-roasted peanuts and often includes salt, sweetener, or emulsifier for texture.
marmalade — Marmalade keeps citrus peel in the preserve, and bitter orange supplies enough pectin for a firm set.
Nutella — Nutella is Ferrero’s sweetened hazelnut-cocoa spread and grew from an earlier product developed by the company.
lemon curd — Lemon curd thickens eggs, sugar, lemon juice and zest with butter into a tart dessert spread or filling.
Vegemite — Vegemite was developed for the Fred Walker Company in 1922 and is eaten in a thin layer because of its strong savoury flavour.
ginger ale — Ginger ale is a carbonated soft drink flavoured with ginger; despite its name, it is not an ale.
tonic water — Tonic water originally carried much more quinine; the modern sweetened drink retains the characteristic bitterness.
root beer — Modern root beer is generally non-alcoholic and carbonated, with commercial flavour replacing unsafe sassafras oil.
cream soda — Cream soda is a family of sweet soft drinks flavoured with vanilla or a cream-like flavour, with many regional versions.
Irn-Bru — Irn-Bru was introduced in 1901 and adopted its unusual spelling after rules required product names to be literally true.
Christmas pudding — Christmas pudding developed from medieval English boiled puddings and traditionally contains dried fruit, suet, breadcrumbs, eggs, and spices.
panettone — Panettone is associated with Milan and has a bread-like texture even though Italians treat it as a dessert.
mooncake — Mooncakes are exchanged among families and friends during the Mid-Autumn Festival and are usually cut into small wedges.
hot cross bun — A hot cross bun marks the end of Lent, and its cross represents the crucifixion of Jesus.
king cake — King-cake traditions vary by country, but many hide a fève and crown or reward the person who finds it.
burrito — A burrito encloses its filling inside a folded flour tortilla, unlike a taco, which is normally left open.
chili con carne — Chili con carne literally means chilli with meat; recipes differ sharply over beans, tomatoes, and seasonings.
quesadilla — Cheese is the defining filling of a quesadilla; the tortilla is then cooked until the filling melts.
enchilada — Enchiladas are filled corn tortillas coated with a savoury chilli sauce; cheese, beans, or meat may be added.
elote — Elote is corn served on the cob with rich, sharp, and spicy toppings; the kernels-only version is often called esquites.
spring roll — Spring rolls vary across Asia, but the familiar Chinese form is a filled wrapper fried to a crisp shell.
sweet and sour pork — Sweet and sour pork combines battered or fried pork with a bright sauce whose sweetness is sharpened by vinegar.
chow mein — Chow mein takes its name from the Taishanese words for stir-fried noodles and has many regional versions.
Kung Pao chicken — Kung Pao chicken is a Sichuan dish whose characteristic combination includes chicken, chillies, and peanuts.
mapo tofu — Mapo tofu balances chilli heat with the numbing quality of Sichuan pepper and the savoury depth of doubanjiang.
pad Thai — Pad Thai balances sour tamarind, salty fish sauce, and sweetness around stir-fried rice noodles.
Thai green curry — Thai green curry uses a fresh green-chilli paste with coconut milk, herbs, and aromatic leaves.
mango sticky rice — Mango sticky rice serves coconut-sweetened glutinous rice with slices of ripe mango.
massaman curry — Massaman curry differs from many Thai curries through its warm dried spices and historical Muslim connections.
larb — Larb combines minced meat with a bright dressing and toasted ground rice that adds aroma and texture.
bibimbap — Bibimbap means mixed rice and brings separately prepared toppings together just before eating.
bulgogi — Bulgogi literally means fire meat and usually uses tender, thinly sliced marinated beef.
tteokbokki — Modern tteokbokki is known for rice cakes in a hot red sauce, often joined by fish cakes and boiled eggs.
japchae — Japchae uses dangmyeon glass noodles, whose sweet-potato starch gives them a springy texture.
samgyeopsal — Samgyeopsal means three-layer flesh, referring to the alternating fat and meat in pork belly.
boeuf bourguignon — Boeuf bourguignon turns beef and Burgundy-style red wine into a long-braised dish with aromatic garnishes.
coq au vin — Coq au vin means rooster in wine, although modern versions commonly use ordinary chicken pieces.
crêpe Suzette — Crêpe Suzette pairs crêpes with beurre Suzette, an orange-butter sauce that may be flambéed at the table.
salade niçoise — Salade niçoise comes from Nice; arguments over cooked vegetables have become part of its culinary fame.
cassoulet — Cassoulet takes its name from the cassole cooking vessel and has famous versions in Castelnaudary, Carcassonne, and Toulouse.
bratwurst — Bratwurst is a family of German sausages whose recipes and seasonings vary strongly by region.
currywurst — Currywurst became a post-war Berlin icon by pairing sausage with curry-seasoned ketchup.
stollen — Stollen is a rich yeast bread whose white sugar coating gives the loaf its snowy festive appearance.
spätzle — Spätzle dough is too soft to roll like pasta, so it is cut, scraped, or pressed into simmering water.
sauerbraten — Sauerbraten means sour roast; its long acidic marinade both flavours and tenderises the meat.
dulce de leche — Dulce de leche develops its colour and flavour as sweetened milk is cooked down over time.
feijoada — Brazilian feijoada commonly combines black beans with several cuts of pork or beef and a full set of side dishes.
brigadeiro — Brigadeiro is cooked until thick enough to shape, then rolled in sprinkles and served in a small paper cup.
lomo saltado — Lomo saltado is a hallmark of Peru’s chifa cuisine, combining wok cookery and soy sauce with local potatoes.
choripán — Choripán contracts the Spanish words for chorizo and bread into the name of this simple sausage sandwich.
phở — Phở is assembled from seasoned broth, rice noodles, herbs, and sliced meat, with garnishes added at the table.
clam chowder — New England clam chowder is the creamy regional style, distinct from Manhattan’s tomato-based version.
vichyssoise — Vichyssoise is a chilled purée whose culinary identity has links to both France and New York.
mulligatawny — Mulligatawny evolved under British colonial influence from a South Indian pepper broth into many hearty soup recipes.
avgolemono — Avgolemono means egg-lemon and relies on tempered eggs for a creamy texture without dairy.
burek — Burek belongs to the broad Ottoman börek family and has distinctive shapes and fillings across the Balkans.
ćevapi — Ćevapi are grilled minced-meat fingers descended from Ottoman kebab traditions and popular across the Balkans.
Shopska salad — The salad’s red tomatoes, green cucumber, and white cheese resemble the red, green, and white colours of Bulgaria’s flag.
ajvar — Ajvar is prepared after the pepper harvest and ranges from mild to hot depending on the chillies used.
pljeskavica — Pljeskavica is a grilled minced-meat patty whose name comes from the action of clapping or patting it into shape.
falafel — Falafel is made from soaked, ground legumes mixed with herbs and spices before frying.
shawarma — Shawarma cooks a cone of meat on a rotating vertical spit, exposing a browned outer layer for slicing.
kibbeh — Kibbeh has baked, fried, and raw forms, but the fried filled croquette is especially recognisable.
manakish — Manakish is often compared with pizza because its seasoned topping is baked directly on a round of dough.
mujaddara — Mujaddara turns inexpensive lentils and grain into a rich dish through a generous topping of caramelised onions.
banana split — A classic banana split arranges vanilla, chocolate, and strawberry ice cream between two banana halves.
cannoli — Cannoli are Sicilian fried pastry shells filled with a sweet ricotta-based cream.
flan — Flan is baked over caramel, then inverted so the caramel becomes its sauce.
Key lime pie — Key lime pie is named for the Florida Keys fruit whose acidity thickens the condensed-milk filling.
Eton mess — Eton mess is linked with Eton College and deliberately keeps its crisp, creamy, and fruity parts in a loose mixture.
yakitori — Yakitori consists of bite-sized chicken pieces grilled on skewers and commonly seasoned with salt or tare.
tonkatsu — Tonkatsu is a breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet traditionally served with shredded cabbage and a thick sauce.
takoyaki — Takoyaki are ball-shaped wheat-batter snacks filled with octopus and associated especially with Osaka.
okonomiyaki — Okonomiyaki is a savoury griddled pancake with cabbage and flexible toppings; its name reflects choosing what one likes.
dorayaki — Dorayaki pairs two small pancake-like cakes with a filling of sweet azuki-bean paste and is famously associated with Doraemon.
khachapuri — Khachapuri is Georgian cheese bread, and Adjarian khachapuri is shaped like a boat with egg and butter in the centre.
khinkali — Khinkali are Georgian dumplings with a pleated wrapper around a juicy meat filling; diners suck out the juices first and leave the tough top uneaten.
plov — Plov is the Central Asian form of pilaf; Uzbek versions commonly combine rice, meat, carrots and onions in a kazan.
beshbarmak — Beshbarmak combines boiled meat with dough, typically egg noodles, and its Turkic name means “five fingers.”
chak-chak — Chak-chak is a Tatar and Bashkir sweet made from fried dough pieces coated and bound with honey.
jollof rice — Jollof rice is a West African one-pot dish based on rice cooked with tomatoes, peppers and aromatics.
suya — Suya is a spicy West African meat skewer, especially associated with Nigeria, seasoned with a peanut-based spice blend.
maafe — Senegalese maafe is a rice-based dish with a creamy peanut-paste sauce.
egusi soup — Egusi soup uses protein-rich ground melon or gourd seeds as its characteristic thickener.
waakye — Waakye is a Ghanaian dish of rice and beans traditionally cooked with red sorghum leaves.
jerk chicken — Jerk chicken is Jamaican chicken seasoned in the jerk style, prominently using allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers.
ackee and saltfish — Ackee and saltfish combines cooked ackee fruit with salt cod and is widely regarded as Jamaica’s national dish.
mofongo — Mofongo is a Puerto Rican plantain dish; modern versions typically fry green pieces before mashing them with garlic, pork, broth and oil.
callaloo — Callaloo is both a Caribbean leafy vegetable and a dish made from greens, with recipes varying by island.
oil down — Oil down is Grenada’s national dish, a coconut-milk stew commonly made with breadfruit, dumplings and salted meat.
crema catalana — Crema catalana is a Catalan custard flavoured with citrus and cinnamon and finished with caramelised sugar.
fabada asturiana — Fabada asturiana is an Asturian bean stew made with fabes and pork products such as chorizo and morcilla.
salmorejo — Salmorejo is a chilled Córdoba soup based on tomato, bread, olive oil and garlic; it is much thicker than gazpacho.
pulpo a feira — Pulpo a feira, also called polbo á feira, is Galician octopus served with oil, salt and paprika.
escalivada — Escalivada is a Catalan preparation of smoky roasted vegetables, especially aubergine and red pepper, dressed with olive oil.
brunost — Brunost is Norwegian brown whey cheese whose characteristic flavour comes from caramelised milk sugars.
Karelian pasty — A Karelian pasty has a thin rye crust around a rice-porridge filling and is often served with egg butter.
smörgåstårta — Smörgåstårta is a Swedish savoury sandwich cake assembled in layers and decorated before serving cold.
kroppkakor — Kroppkakor are Swedish boiled potato dumplings, often filled with pork and onion.
kalakukko — Kalakukko is a Savonian Finnish rye loaf baked with fish and pork sealed inside.
pavlova — Pavlova is a meringue dessert topped with cream and fruit and named after ballerina Anna Pavlova.
ANZAC biscuit — ANZAC biscuits use rolled oats and golden syrup, may include coconut, and are associated with the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
hāngi — Hāngi is a traditional Māori method of cooking food with heated rocks in a covered earth oven.
hokey pokey ice cream — Hokey pokey ice cream is a New Zealand flavour combining vanilla ice cream with pieces of honeycomb toffee.
lolly cake — Lolly cake is a New Zealand sweet made from malt biscuits, confectionery, butter and condensed milk, usually coated in coconut.
Toblerone — Toblerone combines chocolatier Theodor Tobler’s surname with torrone, the Italian word for a type of nougat.
Chupa Chups — Salvador Dalí designed the Chupa Chups logo in 1969.
Häagen-Dazs — Reuben and Rose Mattus founded Häagen-Dazs in the Bronx; Reuben coined its invented Danish-sounding name.
HP Sauce — HP Sauce was named after London’s Houses of Parliament, and its bottle depicts the Palace of Westminster.
Pringles — Pringles dough is formed into saddle shapes and placed in cylindrical cans; the tubular package was designed to reduce breakage and empty air.
La Tomatina — La Tomatina is the annual tomato-throwing festival held in Buñol in Valencia, Spain.
Maslenitsa — Maslenitsa is an East Slavic festival before Lent, celebrated with blini and traditionally ending with an effigy burning.
Battle of the Oranges — The Battle of the Oranges is a carnival tradition in Ivrea, Italy, involving organised teams throwing oranges.
Menton Lemon Festival — Menton’s Lemon Festival, or Fête du Citron, is known for elaborate displays and floats made with citrus fruit.
Night of the Radishes — The Night of the Radishes is an annual Oaxaca event featuring displays carved from oversized radishes.
The Joy of Cooking — The Joy of Cooking preserves Rombauer’s conversational style by presenting recipes as narratives and introducing ingredients when they are needed.
Mastering the Art of French Cooking — Mastering the Art of French Cooking introduced detailed French recipes and techniques to English-speaking home cooks.

assertion: Larousse Gastronomique — Larousse Gastronomique is an encyclopaedia of gastronomy whose first edition focused mainly on French recipes and cooking techniques; later editions broadened its coverage.

Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management — Mrs Beeton’s Book of Household Management is an extensive guide to running a Victorian household, with recipes structured more rigorously than earlier cookbooks.

supportingSource.title: Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management

assertion: Apicius — Apicius is the conventional title of a Roman cookery collection compiled in late antiquity and traditionally associated with Marcus Gavius Apicius.
gumbo — Gumbo is a Louisiana stew thickened in different traditions with roux, okra or filé and made with varied meats or seafood.
jambalaya — Jambalaya is a Louisiana rice dish combining rice with meat, seafood and vegetables in a single pot.
beignet — Louisiana-style beignets are square pieces of leavened dough served with powdered sugar and meant to be eaten immediately after frying.
po' boy — A po’ boy is a Louisiana sandwich on New Orleans French bread, commonly filled with roast beef or fried seafood.
Oysters Rockefeller — Oysters Rockefeller were created at Antoine’s in New Orleans and named for John D. Rockefeller because of their rich sauce.
The Menu — The Menu is an American comedy-horror thriller directed by Mark Mylod and set around an exclusive restaurant on a remote island.
Big Night — Big Night is an American comedy-drama set in the 1950s and co-directed by Campbell Scott and Stanley Tucci.
Tampopo — Tampopo is a Japanese comedy written and directed by Juzo Itami; its nickname plays on the term “spaghetti Western.”
Babette's Feast — Babette's Feast is a Danish drama adapted from Karen Blixen's story and directed by Gabriel Axel.
Eat Drink Man Woman — Eat Drink Man Woman is an Ang Lee film about the Zhu family navigating love, life, tradition and family.
Heston Blumenthal — Heston Blumenthal is an English chef, television personality and food writer whose restaurants include the Fat Duck.
Yotam Ottolenghi — Yotam Ottolenghi is a chef, restaurateur and food writer who co-owns delis and restaurants in London and Bicester Village.
Massimo Bottura — Massimo Bottura is the chef and owner of Osteria Francescana in his native Modena.
Ferran Adrià — Ferran Adrià is a Spanish chef who led El Bulli and often collaborated with his pastry-chef brother Albert Adrià.
Alice Waters — Alice Waters is a chef, restaurateur and food writer who also created the Edible Schoolyard programme in Berkeley.
hibachi — A hibachi is an open-topped heatproof container designed to hold burning charcoal.
kamado — A kamado is a traditional Japanese cook stove fuelled by wood or charcoal.
caquelon — A caquelon may be made from stoneware, ceramic, enamelled cast iron or porcelain and is placed over a burner at the table.
couscoussier — A couscoussier is a double-chambered steamer used in North African and Berber cooking.
donabe — Donabe literally means “earthenware pot”; it is glazed inside, porous outside and used for simmered Japanese dishes.
ceviche — Citrus acid makes the seafood opaque and firm by changing its proteins, but it does not heat-cook the fish.
rollmops — Rollmops are rolled pickled-herring fillets with a savoury filling.
surströmming — Surströmming is a Swedish fermented-herring tradition documented since at least the 16th century.
escabeche — Escabeche has versions in Spanish, Portuguese, Filipino and Hispanic American cuisines, sometimes frying the main ingredient before marinating it.
brandade — Brandade is a speciality of Mediterranean France and is also known in eastern Spain.
Madeira cake — Madeira cake has a firm, light texture and is traditionally flavoured with lemon.
Basque cheesecake — Basque cheesecake was created by La Viña chef-owner Santiago Rivera and gets its custard-like interior from high-temperature baking.
opera cake — Opera cake is assembled in layers and finished with a chocolate glaze.
Dobos torte — The hardened caramel top helped the cake resist drying when refrigeration was limited.
kouign-amann — Kouign-amann is a sweet round Breton bake whose smaller kouignette version resembles a caramelised croissant.
chicken Kyiv — Chicken Kyiv is coated with egg and breadcrumbs and may then be fried or baked.
Brussels sprouts — Their forerunners appeared in northern Europe in the 5th century; cultivation near Brussels in the 13th century gave them their name.
Dijon mustard — Dijon mustard is named for the Burgundian city that became a centre of mustard making in the late Middle Ages.
Parma ham — Parma ham is a protected prosciutto crudo from Emilia-Romagna.
Frankfurter Würstchen — Frankfurter Würstchen is a parboiled smoked sausage traditionally served with bread, mustard, horseradish or potato salad.
full English breakfast — A full breakfast is a substantial cooked meal commonly made in Great Britain and Ireland.
bagel — Bagels are shaped into rings, briefly boiled and then baked, producing their glossy crust and chewy crumb.
pain au chocolat — Pain au chocolat uses the same laminated yeast dough as a croissant, wrapped around chocolate and baked as a rectangle.
kaya toast — Kaya toast is commonly accompanied by soft-boiled eggs and coffee.
çılbır — Çılbır is a Turkish poached-egg dish served with yoghurt, often with garlic mixed into it.
kulfi — Kulfi is often described as traditional Indian ice cream and, unlike ordinary ice cream, is not churned while freezing.
granita — Granita is stirred during freezing to produce a soft mixture of many tiny ice crystals.
Baked Alaska — The oven firms and caramelises the meringue before the ice cream begins to melt.
mochi ice cream — Mochi ice cream is a confection made from Japanese mochi with an ice-cream filling.
semifreddo — Air whipped into semifreddo before freezing gives it a light texture like mousse or soft cake.
poutine — Poutine emerged in Centre-du-Québec and later became a symbol of Québécois culture.
bánh mì — Plain bánh mì is eaten as a staple, while the filled sandwich is called bánh mì thịt.
zapiekanka — Zapiekanka has been a popular Polish street food since the 1970s and is served hot with ketchup.
hotteok — Hotteok is a filled pancake known as a popular street food in South Korea.
jianbing — Jianbing is a popular Chinese street breakfast made with grain-flour batter, eggs, sauces and varied fillings.
pemmican — Europeans in the fur trade and later Arctic and Antarctic explorers adopted pemmican as concentrated high-calorie food.
hardtack — Hardtack is inexpensive and long-lasting if kept dry, and contains little beyond flour and water.
portable soup — Portable soup was an English precursor of meat extract, bouillon cubes and industrial instant food.
Kendal Mint Cake — Kendal Mint Cake originates from Kendal in Cumbria and is flavoured with peppermint.
Erbswurst — Erbswurst was not a true sausage: its portions were crushed into cold water and boiled into creamy pea soup.
beef Stroganoff — This Russian dish became popular around the world in many variations.
beef Wellington — The precise origin of the name is unclear, and its connection to the Duke of Wellington is uncertain.
fettuccine Alfredo — The butter and Parmesan melt and emulsify into a rich sauce that coats the pasta.
Cobb salad — One origin story says Cobb salad became a signature dish of Hollywood's Brown Derby restaurant in 1937.
Lobster Newberg — Legend says an argument between Wenberg and Delmonico led to the dish's name being rearranged from Wenberg to Newberg.
bubble tea — Bubble tea originated in Taiwan in the 1980s and is also called boba.
Earl Grey tea — It has been suggested that the blend was named after Charles Grey, the British prime minister and second Earl Grey.
masala chai — Masala chai adds aromatic herbs and spices to black tea brewed in milk and water.
rooibos — Rooibos is the common name for Aspalathus linearis, a broom-like member of the plant family Fabaceae.
sencha — Sencha is prepared by infusing processed whole leaves in hot water, while matcha mixes powdered tea into water.
spork — Its English name blends the words spoon and fork.
demitasse spoon — A demitasse spoon is smaller than an ordinary teaspoon.
trencher — At the end of a meal, a trencher could be eaten with sauce or given as alms to the poor.
spurtle — Its rod-like shape lets porridge be stirred without congealing and forming lumps.
splayd — William McArthur created the splayd in Sydney in the 1940s.
antipasto — The contents of an antipasto vary greatly by region.
zakuski — Zakuski may include cured fish, meat, salads, pickles and bread.
thali — The Hindi word thali also names the plate on which the meal is served.
banchan — Banchan are set in the middle of the table for diners to share.
pintxo — The Spanish word pincho literally means “thorn” or “spike.”
halloumi — Halloumi has a high melting point and is traditionally made from goat’s and sheep’s milk.
paneer — Paneer is unaged and does not melt when heated.
Gruyère — Gruyère is a hard Swiss cheese whose production begins with raw cow’s milk.
Stilton — Blue Stilton is produced in Derbyshire, Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire.
Pecorino Romano — Pecorino Romano was a staple in the diet of ancient Roman soldiers.
minestrone — Minestrone has no fixed recipe and changes with available seasonal vegetables.
tom yum — In the name, tom refers to boiling while yum means “mixed.”
bouillabaisse — Its broth is traditionally served with rouille on grilled slices of bread.
caldo verde — Caldo verde originated in the Minho region of northern Portugal.
cioppino — Cioppino is traditionally made from the catch of the day, often including crab, clams and fish.
empanada — The name comes from the Spanish verb empanar, meaning to wrap or coat in bread.
samosa — A common samosa filling combines potatoes, onions, peas and spices.
onigiri — Onigiri uses plain rice rather than the vinegared rice associated with sushi.
pupusa — Pupusas can be served with curtido cabbage relish and tomato sauce.
kachori — Kachori may be served with tamarind chutney or mint-and-green-chilli chutney.
shortcrust pastry — Coating flour with fat limits gluten formation, giving shortcrust pastry its tender, crumbly texture.
pâte à choux — Butter, water, flour and eggs give choux pastry enough moisture for steam to puff it during baking.
crème anglaise — Crème anglaise combines sugar and egg yolks with hot milk and is often flavoured with vanilla.
frangipane — Frangipane is commonly made from almonds, butter, sugar and eggs.
sabayon — Sabayon is the French name for the dessert known in Italian as zabaione.
huevos rancheros — Huevos rancheros follows the style of a traditional large mid-morning meal on rural Mexican farms.
nasi lemak — Nasi lemak is widely considered the national dish of Malaysia.
ful medames — In Cairo, huge pots of fava beans were kept simmering to provide breakfast for the city’s population.
appam — Appam is traditionally cooked in an appachatti, a deep pan shaped like a wok.
upma — Upma variations add or remove spices and vegetables.
surimi — Sucrose and other carbohydrates can act as cryoprotectants by stabilising surimi protein during freezing.
lutefisk — Lutefisk develops a distinctive gelatinous texture during its treatment.
katsuobushi — Katsuobushi is shaved into flakes and used with kombu to make dashi.
bacalhau — Drying and salting cod preserve its nutrients and change the fish’s taste.
bottarga — Bottarga is commonly made from grey mullet or bluefin tuna roe.
umami — In 1908, Kikunae Ikeda identified umami as a distinct taste attributed to glutamic acid.
monosodium glutamate — Monosodium glutamate produces an umami taste through its glutamate component.
shiitake — Shiitake grows naturally on the decaying wood of deciduous trees and is widely cultivated.
kombu — Kombu is widely eaten in East Asia and is one of three main ingredients used to make dashi.
yeast extract — Yeast extract contains the amino acid glutamic acid and is used in spreads, soups and seasonings.
Thermos — In the United States, lowercase “thermos” was declared a genericised trademark in 1963.
Tupperware — Earl Tupper introduced the product line in 1946.
Pyrex — Pyrex was originally made from borosilicate glass.
Mason jar — John Landis Mason patented the preserving jar in 1858; its threaded mouth accepts a metal band that presses down a separate lid.
Crock-Pot — The Rival Company introduced the Crock-Pot name for its slow cooker in 1971.
bunny chow — Bunny chow originated in Durban and turns a hollowed loaf into an edible container for curry.
fufu — Fufu was originally made from boiled cassava, plantains and cocoyam.
arepa — Arepas are made from ground maize dough and may be baked, grilled or fried.
ugali — Ugali is cooked in boiling water or milk until it reaches a firm consistency.
sadza — Sadza is commonly rolled into a ball by hand before being dipped into sauce, sour milk or stewed vegetables.
